# Introduction

Forecasting tools can make it easy to generate predictions, but understanding how they work helps us decide when to rely on them. Different workloads have different patterns, and a model that works well for one may be less useful for another. In this post, I'll explore two forecasting approaches in R and test how well they predict phone volume.

Accurate phone forecasts can help teams balance phone coverage with other work and plan time for training, staff meetings, or system updates. Here, I'll use hourly counts of recorded inquiries to New York City's 311 call center to explore daily, weekly, and yearly patterns and test predictions against later observations.

I'll start with Prophet, which models trends and recurring patterns and can incorporate holidays or other predictors. Then I'll explore ETS (Error, Trend, Seasonality), an exponential smoothing approach that gives more weight to recent observations. I'll compare their predictions against actual call volumes and finish with a recommendation for this dataset, including the limitations of that comparison.

# Set-up

## Packages

I'll use these packages throughout the post:

- **tidyverse:** import, clean, summarize, and visualize the data. It includes readr, dplyr, tidyr, and ggplot2.
- **lubridate:** work with dates and times and create calendar features.
- **httr2:** request data directly from NYC Open Data.
- **prophet:** build forecasts with trend, seasonal patterns, and optional holiday effects.
- **forecast:** build ETS models and calculate forecast accuracy measures.
- **plotly:** make charts interactive so we can inspect individual dates and predictions.

Install these packages once if needed, then load them when starting the analysis. The installation line is commented out so rendering will not reinstall them.

## Data

The [NYC 311 Call Center Inquiry dataset](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/311-Call-Center-Inquiry/wewp-mm3p/about_data) records agent-handled inquiries, including a date and time, topic, and resolution. For this analysis, I'll request hourly record counts from January 2015 through December 2018. This gives us three years for initial training and a later full year to test the forecasts against actual recorded activity.

The request groups records by date and hour before downloading, keeping the file manageable. I'll save the extract locally so future runs can reuse it. The resulting fields are `date`, `hour`, and `inquiry_count`. These counts describe recorded agent-handled activity, rather than all incoming demand or abandoned calls. We'll check gaps and counting rules before modeling; an absent hour is not automatically zero.

I chose a period before 2020 because NYC notes that pandemic-related handling changes caused underreporting from March 2020 onward.

```{r setup}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide

# Run once if these packages are not installed:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "lubridate", "httr2",
#                    "prophet", "forecast", "plotly"))

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(httr2)
library(prophet)
library(forecast)
library(plotly)

# Reuse the saved extract after the first download.
data_path <- "data/nyc_311_hourly_2015_2018.csv"
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

if (!file.exists(data_path)) {
  request <- httr2::request(
    "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/wewp-mm3p.csv"
  ) |>
    req_url_query(
      `$select` = paste(
        "date_trunc_ymd(date_time) AS date,",
        "date_extract_hh(date_time) AS hour,",
        "count(*) AS inquiry_count"
      ),
      `$where` = paste(
        "date_time >= '2015-01-01T00:00:00'",
        "AND date_time < '2019-01-01T00:00:00'"
      ),
      `$group` = "date,hour",
      `$order` = "date,hour",
      `$limit` = 100000
    ) |>
    req_timeout(seconds = 180)

  response <- req_perform(request)
  writeBin(resp_body_raw(response), data_path)
}

data <- read_csv(
  data_path,
  col_types = cols(
    date = col_character(),
    hour = col_integer(),
    inquiry_count = col_double()
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE,
  progress = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(date = ymd(substr(date, 1, 10))) |>
  arrange(date, hour)

# Check the basic structure without printing results.
stopifnot(
  nrow(data) > 0,
  all(c("date", "hour", "inquiry_count") %in% names(data)),
  !anyNA(data),
  all(data$hour >= 0 & data$hour <= 23),
  all(data$inquiry_count >= 0),
  !anyDuplicated(data[c("date", "hour")])
)
```

# Breif EDA & Cleaning

## Calls Offered by Service

I'm starting by looking at the number of calls offered for each service. 

```{r offered by q}
offer_by_q <- data |>
  group_by(`Service Name`) |>
  summarise(`Calls Offered` = sum(`Calls Offered`, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(`Calls Offered`))
offer_by_q
```

## Calls Offered for Each Payment Related Services

I am not sure what all the queues are, but see 'payment' in here. Lets focus our analysis on payment lines. 

```{r}
payment_data <- data |>
  filter(str_detect(`Service Name`, regex("payment", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  group_by(`Service Name`) |>
  summarise(`Calls Offered` = sum(`Calls Offered`, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(`Calls Offered`))
payment_data
```

For payments, it looks like customers can call in to reach:

* Make Payment: Caller is trying to make a payment.

* Make Payment Error: Caller had an issue while making a payment.

* Payments Off: Payment option may have been unavailable, and caller was routed here.

I am also going to assume the 'E' is for English lines and 'S' is for Spanish lines. 

## Calls Offered for All Payment Services

To somewhat simplify this analysis, lets start by looking at calls offed for all payment services as a whole. 

```{r payment monthly}
payment_monthly <- data |>
  mutate(`Reporting Date` = as_date(parse_date_time(`Reporting Date`, orders = c("ymd", "mdy")))) |>
  filter(str_detect(`Service Name`, regex("payment", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  group_by(`Reporting Date`) |>
  summarise(`Calls Offered` = sum(`Calls Offered`, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(`Reporting Date`))

payment_monthly
```

# Visualize Payments by Month 

Lets look at payments by month, and compare each year. 

```{r payment monthly yoy}
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-width: 8
payment_monthly |>
  mutate(
    year = year(`Reporting Date`),
    month = month(`Reporting Date`, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = `Calls Offered`)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = `Calls Offered`), vjust = -0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Payment Calls Offered by Month",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Calls Offered"
  )
```

Right away we can see a large range of calls between 1,502 and 6,491 since 2018. It also looks like call volume has been decreasing the last couple of years compared to pre-pandemic call volumes. 

# Last 5 Years Summary Stats

It looks like we are missing some data in 2021 from March - May. Lets filter out anything before June 2021 and observe the summary stats. 

```{r}
payment_monthly <- payment_monthly |>
  filter(`Reporting Date` >= as.Date("2021-06-01"))
summary(payment_monthly)
```

Cool! It looks like over the past 5 years Meza gets about 2k calls a month related to payments with a range of about 1k calls. 

## Visualize Payments by Quarter

Looks by month, I am not seeing obvious consistent spikes or dips in the data so I am going to look at it by quarter to see if there if there might be any seasonal trends. 

```{r}
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-width: 8
payment_quarterly <- payment_monthly |>
  mutate(
    year = year(`Reporting Date`),
    quarter = paste0("Q", quarter(`Reporting Date`))
  ) |>
  group_by(year, quarter) |>
  summarise(`Calls Offered` = sum(`Calls Offered`, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

payment_quarterly |>
  ggplot(aes(x = quarter, y = `Calls Offered`)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = `Calls Offered`), vjust = -0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title = "Payment Calls Offered by Quarter",
    x = "Quarter",
    y = "Calls Offered"
  )
```

I am not seeing any seasonal trends that are too obvious. Perhaps there is a dip in quarter three, but I will be curious to see what our forecast comes up with for the next few months (Q3) of 2026. 

## Prepare for Prophet

Now we need to slightly modify our data for the Prophet model. Mainly just changing the column headers. 

```{r}
prophet_payment <- payment_monthly |>
  transmute(
    ds = `Reporting Date`,
    y = `Calls Offered`
  ) |>
  arrange(ds)
```


# Prophet

```{r}
# model data
model_prophet <- prophet(
  prophet_payment,
  weekly.seasonality = FALSE,
  daily.seasonality = FALSE
)
# forecast the next 12 month
future <- make_future_dataframe(
  model_prophet,
  periods = 12,
  freq = "month"
)
# generate forecast
forecast <- predict(model_prophet, future)
# plot
plot(model_prophet, forecast) |>
  ggplotly()
```


```{r}
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-width: 8
# modify data
forecast_yoy <- forecast |>
  select(ds, yhat, yhat_lower, yhat_upper) |>
  left_join(prophet_payment, by = "ds") |>
  mutate(
    `Calls Offered` = if_else(is.na(y), yhat, y),
    type = if_else(is.na(y), "Forecast", "Actual"),
    year = year(ds),
    month = month(ds, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)
  )
# plot 
forecast_yoy |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = `Calls Offered`, fill = type)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(`Calls Offered`)), vjust = -0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title = "Payment Calls Offered Forecast by Month",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Calls Offered",
    fill = NULL
  ) 
```
